data.name: Audio Forager
data.detailed_description:
Feel the magic of Machine Learning in this new experiment that combines over 44,000 sounds from Freesound, a data set created by Kyle McDonald and a touch of Cabbibo weirdness.

Run your hands through a cloud of sound, learn the shape of the computers mind, select your favorite audio delicacies and make a drum set from this decadent aural smorgasbord.

The mechanics may be simple ( navigate through a 3D map of sounds , select individual sounds to keep, and hit those sounds again to play them ), but because of absolutely massive size of the data set, the possibilities are endless!

Want to create your own piano out of synth notes? Go ahead!
How about a marimba of pops and crackles? Be my guest!

And if you are just the exploring type, the data is beautiful enough to begin with! There is no need to make an instrument, or play it, because in from of you lies a tool for discovering and understanding a beautiful algorithm, and even more beautiful data: Sound

This project would not be possible without the amazing community of FreeSound.org
As well as Kyle McDonald, who scraped audio from freesound.org & made t-SNE embeddings of the data!

Created during Unity Artist in Residency 2017

reviews.review:
Audio Forager is an unconventional virtual reality experience that treats sound itself as an explorable environment. Instead of relying on combat, storytelling, puzzles, or traditional progression systems, it invites players to wander through a huge collection of audio samples and discover relationships between them. Developed and published by Cabbibo, the project sits somewhere between an experimental game, an interactive sound installation, and a creative musical tool. Its unusual approach makes it considerably more specialized than an ordinary VR title, but it also gives the experience an identity that is difficult to confuse with anything else.

The defining feature is its enormous library of more than 44,000 sounds originating from the Freesound community. Rather than presenting this material through conventional folders or lists, Audio Forager transforms the collection into a three-dimensional space. Machine-learning techniques help organize sounds according to their characteristics, allowing the player to move around this unusual sonic landscape and encounter related samples through exploration. The result is an inventive method of making a massive audio dataset feel tangible. Instead of searching for a particular recording by name, players can effectively wander until something interesting catches their ears.

Interaction revolves around discovering, selecting, and playing sounds. Individual samples can be collected and subsequently used as components of improvised musical arrangements. A player could gather melodic tones and attempt to assemble something resembling an instrument, or search for percussive noises and create a personalized drum kit. Environmental recordings, electronic sounds, voices, effects, and stranger samples can also produce unpredictable combinations. There is no requirement to make polished music, which is important because experimentation is far more central to the experience than musical accomplishment.

This freedom gives Audio Forager a surprisingly playful character despite its technical foundations. Players can spend their time deliberately searching for useful samples, but aimless exploration can be equally entertaining. Discovering an unexpected cluster of noises and experimenting with the results becomes its own reward. It encourages curiosity rather than efficiency, and some of its best moments come from stumbling across sounds that would probably never have been intentionally searched for in a traditional audio database.

Virtual reality contributes substantially to the concept. Audio Forager was created around VR interaction, making the process of navigating and manipulating sound feel physical rather than purely menu driven. Moving through a spatial representation of thousands of samples gives the project a sense of scale that would be difficult to reproduce through an ordinary desktop interface. The abstract presentation also suits the subject matter because elaborate realistic environments would arguably distract from the relationship between position and audio. Here, visualization exists primarily to help turn an otherwise abstract dataset into a place the player can understand through movement and listening.

The downside is that its experimental nature also defines its limitations. There is little resemblance to a conventional campaign, with no substantial narrative structure, character development, competitive system, or traditional sequence of challenges. Players who need objectives and rewards to maintain motivation may exhaust the novelty fairly quickly. The huge number of available sounds provides extraordinary content variety, but the underlying interaction remains relatively simple. Long-term enjoyment consequently depends heavily on how much pleasure the player gets from sound experimentation and self-directed discovery.

Its strongest audience is likely to include experimental musicians, audio enthusiasts, sound designers, technology enthusiasts, and VR users interested in unusual interactive projects. There is also an interesting educational quality to the experience. Audio Forager demonstrates how a massive collection of information can be computationally organized and represented spatially, turning concepts associated with machine learning and data visualization into something immediately interactive. Players do not need a technical background to appreciate this aspect because the underlying idea is communicated naturally through exploration.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively unsuitable for normal handheld play. Audio Forager is fundamentally designed around PC virtual reality and requires VR hardware and tracked interaction rather than functioning as a conventional controller-based Steam Deck game. Even if compatibility layers can technically launch portions of the software under certain configurations, that should not be confused with practical native Steam Deck support. Anyone considering it specifically for portable Deck gaming should therefore regard it as unsupported for the intended experience. Its hardware requirements place it firmly in the PC VR category rather than among games designed for handheld use.

The minimalist mechanical structure means Audio Forager should be judged primarily on whether its central experiment works, and in that respect it succeeds. Converting tens of thousands of community-created recordings into an environment that can be wandered through is a genuinely inventive concept. The ability to collect discoveries and transform them into playable sound combinations adds enough creativity to prevent the experience from being merely a visualization demonstration. It becomes a sandbox where browsing, listening, experimentation, and improvisation overlap.

Audio Forager ultimately offers something fascinating but deliberately niche. It does not provide enough conventional gameplay systems to satisfy players searching for a substantial VR adventure, yet that was never really its purpose. As an interactive exploration of sound, machine-assisted organization, and spontaneous music creation, it possesses considerable originality. Its greatest achievement is making an enormous and potentially intimidating collection of audio feel like a strange world waiting to be explored rather than a database waiting to be searched.

The limited traditional gameplay and dependence on VR equipment narrow its audience, but its creative interpretation of sound exploration, enormous sample collection, and experimental musical possibilities make it a memorable project for players interested in the intersection of audio, technology, and virtual reality.

Rating: 7/10
